UTI is a direct physical-capacity candidate across trades and Concorde healthcare programs; track campus opening cadence, student starts, placement rates, and employer/manufacturer partnerships.

HSTM is not proven as a clinical-placement platform, but it is a speculative-shadow software/data candidate tied to credentialing, clinical development, compliance, scheduling, and nursing-school workflows.

The most direct clinical-placement software vendors appear likely to be private or embedded inside broader healthcare education/workforce SaaS; next pass should search private competitors to map whether any public consolidator owns comparable assets.
HSTM should be promoted for deeper Layer 2 verification as the most direct public-market candidate tied to clinical placement software and healthcare workforce compliance infrastructure.
UTI is a plausible underfollowed capacity beneficiary because Concorde adds healthcare campus/lab/clinical-experience exposure to a company still often perceived as technical/automotive training.
APEI is a speculative-shadow candidate: nursing education assets are relevant, but clinical placement capacity and segment-level economics require verification before upgrading.
The node appears investable through three public-market paths: clinical placement/compliance software, physical healthcare career colleges, and employer/hospital partnership networks.

Many pure simulation-equipment vendors and clinical-placement networks are private; CAE exited healthcare simulation in 2024, so public exposure may be indirect or embedded inside education/workforce software names.
HSTM should be promoted for deeper Layer 2 review as the most direct underfollowed clinical-placement software and healthcare compliance-documentation asset found in this pass.
UTI is a relevant hands-on capacity operator because Concorde adds healthcare campus and clinical-placement exposure while legacy UTI adds trade-school lab and employer-partner exposure.

Clinical placement and simulation capacity are not pure online-learning exposures; the bottleneck appears to be offline throughput, compliance documentation, employer/health-system partnerships, and accredited lab capacity.

The most direct clinical-placement software assets are mostly private or embedded inside broader public companies; later layers should verify whether HSTM's acquired clinical-rotation products are financially material.

HSTM should be retained for Layer 2 as the cleanest direct clinical-placement workflow candidate; evidence priority is product-level revenue or usage growth for myClinicalExchange, TCPS, and The Clinical Hub.

UTI is a plausible underfollowed physical-capacity beneficiary through Concorde healthcare programs and UTI/MIAT skilled-trades campuses; verify whether campus capacity, employer agreements, and externship/clinical placement are actual constraints.

LINC is a more speculative small-cap hands-on training candidate; include only if later evidence shows healthcare-services or skilled-trades capacity additions with measurable employer demand and placement outcomes.

Clinical placement and hands-on training capacity may be a shadow bottleneck because online education demand can scale faster than hospital rotations, lab seats, instructors, accreditation approvals, and employer sites.

summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Layer 1B expansion found four US-listed public companies with plausible direct or second-order exposure to the hands-on capacity bottleneck in education/workforce training. The cleanest direct capacity names are Adtalem and Grand Canyon Education through healthcare/nursing education, clinical affiliations, off-campus labs, and employer-linked pathways. Universal Technical Institute adds hands-on trade and healthcare campus capacity via UTI and Concorde. HealthStream is the software/compliance layer: not a placement network pure-play, but exposed to healthcare workforce development, credentialing, scheduling, clinical development, nursing schools, and direct-to-student networks. No buy/sell view is implied. Layer 1B expansion focused on the offline and compliance-constrained capacity layer behind online/workforce education: clinical rotations, nursing/allied-health campuses, trade-school labs, employer partnerships, and healthcare workforce credentialing/training systems. The cleanest underfollowed candidate found is HealthStream because it explicitly acquired clinical-rotation management assets. UTI and APEI provide campus/lab/clinical capacity exposure through healthcare and technical training assets. Adtalem is included as a reference/context anchor because it is a more visible healthcare-education provider with hospital partnerships and clinical rotations, but it is less of a hidden supplier than a direct demand beneficiary.
